name: Q-switched / picosecond laser for pigment

card.summary: Ultra-short-pulse lasers used in clinics to break up pigment such as sun spots, melasma and tattoo ink; clinic-based, with limited published trial detail.
card.aka: Q-switched Nd:YAG, alexandrite, ruby; picosecond laser; PicoSure, PicoWay
card.note: Pigment changes after treatment are common and more likely in darker skin types.

quick.overview:
Q-switched lasers deliver very short, high-energy pulses, and picosecond lasers deliver even shorter ones. Dermatologists use them to target pigment in the skin, including tattoo ink and, in clinics, brown spots such as lentigines and melasma.
Registered trials of picosecond lasers exist for melasma, wrinkles and skin tightening, but results are not summarised here, so the evidence for the appearance uses is limited.
quick.mechanism: Pigment particles absorb the laser light in nanoseconds or picoseconds, heat rapidly and fragment, and the body then clears the smaller pieces via macrophages and the lymphatic system. Encyclopedic sources describe the effect as selective photothermolysis with a photomechanical shock component, sparing surrounding tissue.
quick.risks: About half of tattoo-removal patients have temporary pigment changes that usually resolve within 6 to 12 months, and these are more likely in skin types IV to VI. Hypopigmentation, paradoxical darkening of some inks, rare scarring and very rare blistering are reported.

lead: Q-switched and picosecond lasers are pulsed lasers whose very short pulses are used in dermatology to fragment pigment. Q-switched devices emit pulses in the nanosecond range; picosecond devices are shorter still. Both are used for tattoo removal and, in clinics, for pigmented skin lesions such as lentigines and melasma.[1]

Commercial Q-switched lasers emerged in the late 1980s, following early research in Glasgow in the early 1980s. Wavelengths in common use include 532, 694, 755 and 1064 nanometres, chosen to match the target colour and skin type.[1]

For the appearance uses on this page, published trial detail is limited. Clinical trial registrations exist for picosecond lasers in melasma, wrinkles and skin tightening, but their outcomes are not summarised here.[2][3][4][5]

For appearance, the practical draw is that the same pulsed-light principle used on tattoos is applied to brown spots and uneven tone: dermatology clinics use these lasers to break up pigment in sun spots (lentigines) and, for some patients, melasma, aiming for a more even complexion.[1][8][11] A picosecond laser was introduced in 2013 on the basis of clinical research that appeared to show better clearance of hard-to-remove colours such as green and light blue ink.[11]

paras: Targets absorb the light and heat faster than heat can spread to nearby tissue, a principle called selective photothermolysis. A photomechanical shock wave then helps break the pigment into fragments, which are cleared by immune cells and the lymphatic system.[1]

Four factors are described as determining success: penetration depth, wavelength absorption by the target, pulse duration and energy per pulse.[1] Multiple wavelengths are used because different colours absorb differently, and the 1064 nm wavelength is described as suitable for darker skin and black ink.[1]

Picosecond systems are the newer category. A 2017 study used multiphoton microscopy to examine picosecond-laser-induced optical breakdown in human skin in vivo.[6] Encyclopedic sources describe anecdotal claims that picosecond lasers clear ink faster.[1]

Tattoo removal is the best-documented use, and Q-switched lasers are described as the standard modern method.[1] A laboratory analysis of 41 tattoo pigment compounds examined their chemical structure and absorption spectra to understand why coloured tattoos respond unpredictably.[7]

Cosmetic lentigines and melasma are the pigment uses that matter for appearance culture. Melasma is a chronic, relapsing condition for which a general reference lists lasers such as KTP among procedural options and states that treatments are often unsatisfying.[8]

In tattoo removal about half of patients have temporary pigment changes that usually resolve within 6 to 12 months, and these are more likely in skin types IV to VI. Hypopigmentation is more frequent in darker skin and with higher energy or more frequent sessions. Scarring is rare and large blisters are very rare. Paradoxical darkening can occur, especially with white, flesh-tone, pink and makeup inks.[1]
A case report described successful treatment of treatment-resistant laser-induced pigment darkening of a cosmetic tattoo.[9]

Q-switching is a technique for making a laser emit short, very intense pulses by holding back the beam inside the resonator while the gain medium stores energy, then releasing it all at once as a giant pulse. It was proposed in 1958 by Gordon Gould and demonstrated in 1961 or 1962 by Robert Hellwarth and F. J. McClung at Hughes Research Laboratories using a ruby laser and electrically switched Kerr-cell shutters.[11] The effect is produced either actively, with an externally controlled attenuator such as an electro-optic or acousto-optic modulator, or passively, with a saturable absorber such as Cr:YAG used with Nd:YAG lasers.[11]

A typical Q-switched Nd:YAG laser with a 10 cm resonator can emit pulses of several tens of nanoseconds, with kilowatt peak powers even when average power is under a watt.[11] The same source notes that Nd:YAG lasers are the most favoured type for tattoo removal because of their high peak power, high repetition rates and relatively low cost.[11] Picosecond systems shorten the pulse further, which proponents say shifts the effect toward photomechanical shattering rather than heating.[1][6]

Wikipedia notes that Q-switched lasers can be used to remove dark spots and other pigmentation problems as well as tattoos.[11] In the cosmetic setting this means flat brown lentigines and similar discrete lesions, where the melanin in the spot absorbs the pulse and is fragmented, then cleared by the body.[1][11]

Melasma, a patchy brown discoloration, is a different problem. A general reference describes it as a chronic, relapsing condition for which treatments are often unsatisfying, and lasers appear among the procedural options rather than as a settled first choice.[8] A registered 40-person trial examined a picosecond Nd:YAG laser with 1,064 and 595 nm wavelengths in melasma.[2]

In tattoo removal, the full course is described as six to twenty treatments depending on ink amount and colour, spaced at least a month apart and using different wavelengths for different colours.[11]

sections.h: Pigmentation concerns the laser is used for
paras: Solar lentigines, often called sun spots or age spots, are flat light-brown to dark benign marks that appear on sun-exposed areas such as the face, hands, shoulders and forearms after years of ultraviolet exposure.[12] Reference summaries describe them as usually a cosmetic rather than a medical concern, with treatment options that include cryotherapy, electrosurgery, laser treatment and topical depigmenting agents such as hydroquinone, tretinoin and azelaic acid.[12] Dermatology references note that they only occasionally obscure the detection of skin cancer, which is one reason clinicians examine marks before treating them.[12]

Melasma, a patchy facial pigmentation linked to sun exposure and hormones, is another condition for which picosecond and low-fluence approaches have been registered for study, though it is known for recurring and for sometimes worsening after heat-based treatments.[8][2]

Q-switched lasers emit nanosecond pulses, and later picosecond systems emit pulses a thousand times shorter, which concentrates energy into a more mechanical, less thermal effect on pigment particles.[11][6] Tattoo-removal references describe Q-switched devices as the established standard and note that outcomes depend on pigment colour, depth, skin type and the wavelength used; an Nd:YAG at 1064 nm penetrates deeper and is the wavelength more commonly associated with darker skin, whereas shorter wavelengths target different pigments.[1][11] Registered trials have examined 1064 and 595 nm picosecond Nd:YAG for melasma, a picosecond laser for tattoo clearance, and fractional 1064 nm picosecond laser for facial pigmentation and wrinkles.[2][3][10]

sections.h: Skin of colour and risk of pigment change
paras: Pigment-specific lasers can themselves change pigment. In tattoo removal, reference summaries state that about half of patients have temporary pigment changes that usually resolve within 6 to 12 months, with hypopigmentation more frequent in darker skin types and with higher energy or more frequent sessions.[1] A case report in the literature describes treatment-resistant laser-induced pigment darkening that was eventually treated successfully with a Q-switched laser, illustrating that the same device is used both to cause and to resolve pigment disturbances in some patients.[9]

Trial registrations include a completed 40-person study of 1,064 and 595 nm picosecond Nd:YAG laser for melasma (started 2016), a completed 60-person trial of a picosecond laser for unwanted tattoos (started 2013), two completed 20-person studies of a picosecond laser with a lens array for wrinkles (started 2013), and a 30-person study of fractional 1,064 nm picosecond laser for facial skin tightening (started 2023, status unknown).[2][3][4][5][10] Published results from these registrations are not summarised here.
Search hits on Q-switched lasers in rheumatoid arthritis, fibre-laser physics and dental enamel concern unrelated uses and are not discussed.

timeline.event: Glasgow research on laser tattoo removal.[1]
Multi-wavelength lasers begin covering more ink colours.[1]
Registered picosecond trials for tattoos and wrinkles begin.[3][4][5]
